sources.text:
Final-year group project, four of us, Sept 2025 to March 2026. We built a self-service GPU job runner for the department's machine learning teaching cluster. Students submitted training jobs through a small web form and the runner queued them on Kubernetes (k3s on six old lab workstations with GPUs).

Stack: Python and FastAPI for the API, Redis for the queue, Helm charts for deploys, Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring.

Big decision: we used Kubernetes Jobs with a scheduler extender instead of Slurm, because the department wanted everything in containers and we needed per-course GPU quotas.

Problem: in week 9 jobs started dying at random, pods OOMKilled even with tiny models. Took us three days. Turned out the default /dev/shm in the pods was 64 MB, so the PyTorch data loaders crashed. Fixed it by mounting a memory-backed emptyDir with a size limit per job.

Result: 140 students used it in the spring term and the average wait for a GPU went from about two days (the old sign-up sheet) to under 20 minutes.

Learned: check the node's kernel log first. dmesg showed the OOM kills straight away and we wasted two days before looking.

Why Graphcore: I liked the infrastructure side of the project more than the machine learning side, and Graphcore builds both the hardware and the cloud platform that models run on.
I wrote the Helm patch that mounted a memory-backed emptyDir with a size limit per job.

Our four-person final-year team built a GPU job runner for the department's machine learning teaching cluster, from September 2025 to March 2026. 140 students used it in the spring term and the average wait for a GPU went from about two days to under 20 minutes.

Students submitted training jobs through a small web form and the runner queued them on Kubernetes (k3s on six old lab workstations with GPUs). The stack used Python and FastAPI for the API, Redis for the queue, Helm charts for deploys, and Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring.

We used Kubernetes Jobs with a scheduler extender instead of Slurm because the department wanted everything in containers and we needed per-course GPU quotas.

In week 9 jobs started dying at random, pods OOMKilled even with tiny models, and it took us three days to resolve. Investigation showed the default /dev/shm in the pods was 64 MB, so the PyTorch data loaders crashed. We learned to check the node's kernel log first, as dmesg showed the OOM kills straight away and we had wasted two days before looking. The issue was fixed by mounting a memory-backed emptyDir with a size limit per job. Sam wrote the Helm patch. I reproduced the failure, tested his fix and wrote the incident notes.

Dear Graphcore hiring team,

I am applying for the Graduate Cloud Platform Engineer 2027 role at Graphcore.

We built a self-service GPU job runner for the department's machine learning teaching cluster. I liked the infrastructure side of the project more than the machine learning side, and Graphcore builds both the hardware and the cloud platform that models run on. Students submitted training jobs through a small web form and the runner queued them on Kubernetes (k3s on six old lab workstations with GPUs).

The stack used Python and FastAPI for the API, Redis for the queue, Helm charts for deploys, and Prometheus and Grafana for monitoring. In week 9 jobs started dying at random, pods OOMKilled even with tiny models, because the default /dev/shm in the pods was 64 MB so the PyTorch data loaders crashed. The issue was fixed by mounting a memory-backed emptyDir with a size limit per job. Sam wrote the Helm patch. I reproduced the failure, tested his fix and wrote the incident notes. 140 students used it in the spring term and the average wait for a GPU went from about two days (the old sign-up sheet) to under 20 minutes.

Thank you for considering my application.

Kind regards, Ellie
